title: Fork Process Memory & Copy-on-Write Transfer
prompt: A Python script initializes a global list `items = [1, 2, 3]` and spawns a child process using `os.fork()`. The child modifies `items.append(4)`. Does the parent process see `4` in `items`? Explain why in terms of address spaces and memory sharing.

forbidden_misconceptions: child modification directly alters parent list
global variables are shared across processes
evaluator_rubric.scoring_criteria: Learner must state that the parent will NOT see 4. After fork, child and parent have distinct virtual address spaces. Even with copy-on-write optimization, modifications allocate a new physical page for the child, keeping parent memory untouched.
evaluator_rubric.ideal_response_summary: The parent process does NOT see 4. Upon fork, the operating system creates a distinct virtual address space for the child process. Although pages are initially shared read-only via copy-on-write (COW), when the child appends to the list, the OS allocates a new private page for the child. The parent's heap remains completely unmodified.
